parole.significato: A person who abbreviates or shortens.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin abbreviātor. Compare French abbréviateur.

parole.significato: One of the functionaries who light and trim the tapers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin accēnsor, from accendō (“light, kindle”) + -tor (agent noun suffix). Compare accend.

parole.significato: Synonym of alb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin alba (“alb”), from Latin alba (as in tunica alba (“white tunic”), vestis alba (“white garment”)), feminine of albus (“white”). Doublet of alb.

parole.significato: At the end of a religious prayer: so be it.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English amen, from Old English āmen, from Ecclesiastical Latin āmēn, from Ancient Greek ἀμήν (amḗn), from Biblical Hebrew אָמֵן (ʾāmēn, “certainly, verily”) (cognate with Arabic آمِينَ (ʔāmīna), Classical Syriac ܐܡܝܢ (ʾāmên)). In Old English, it was used only at the end of the

parole.significato: An abbess or spiritual mother, especially one of the Desert Mothers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin amma, from Classical Syriac ܐܸܡܵܐ (ʾemmā, “mother, abbess”).

parole.significato: The spiritual or mystical interpretation of a word or passage beyond the literal, allegorical or moral sense.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin anagōgē, from Ancient Greek ἀναγωγή (anagōgḗ, “religious or ecstatic elevation, mystical feeling”), from ἀνάγειν (anágein, “lift up”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + ἄγειν (ágein, “to lead”).

parole.significato: A religious confraternity that, as a special concession of the Holy See, can join or affiliate with, and extend privile…
parole.testo: From arch- + confraternity, calque of Ecclesiastical Latin archiconfrāternitās.

parole.significato: An inhabitant of the island and city of Arwad.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin Aradium, from Ancient Greek Ἀράδιον (Arádion), from Biblical Hebrew אַרְוָדִי ('arvāḏî) , gentilic of Biblical Hebrew אַרְוַד ('arvaḏ) . Compare Phoenician 𐤀𐤓𐤅𐤃 (ʾrwd) and Ancient Greek Ἄραδος (Árados).

parole.significato: An implement, in the form of a brush or of a rod with a perforated container, for sprinkling holy water; a holy-water s…
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin aspergillum, from aspergō (“to sprinkle”).

parole.significato: A designated space within a church, or a separate room or building associated with a church, where a baptismal font is…
parole.testo: From Middle English baptistery, baptisterie, from Ecclesiastical Latin baptistērium, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστήριον (baptistḗrion); equivalent to baptism + -ry.

parole.significato: A short invocation for help, blessing and guidance from God, said on behalf of another person or persons (sometimes at…
parole.testo: From Middle English benediccion, from Ecclesiastical Latin benedictio, benedictionis, from benedictus (“blessed; well spoken of”). Doublet of benison.

parole.significato: The Gospel canticle of Zechariah (Luke 1:68–79), with the incipit Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel (“Blessed be the Lord…
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin benedictus (“blessed, praised”), from benedīcō (“to speak well (of)”).

parole.significato: The dignity and ecclesiastic office of Roman Catholic cardinal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin cardinālātus, from cardinālis (“cardinal”) + -ātus, itself the noun use of an adjective derived from cardō (“hinge, main point”) + -ālis (“-al”). By surface analysis, cardinal + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

parole.significato: The prayer said before the reading of the epistle lesson, especially one found in a prayerbook, as with the Book of Com…
parole.testo: From Middle English collecte, from Ecclesiastical Latin collēcta (“assembly; collect”), originally designating the gathering at the beginning of a liturgical celebration.

parole.significato: Any of the people engaged in a conversation.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin collocūtor. First attested in 1620.

parole.significato: A rebel organization characterized by religious fanaticism.
parole.testo: Clipping of Ecclesiastical Latin in saecula saeculōrum (“for ever and ever”). Compare Tagalog kolorum.

parole.significato: Followed by with: to express condolence to, or sympathetic sorrow with, someone; to lament in sympathy with someone.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱóm Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin condolēre, the present active infinitive of condoleō (“to feel severe pain, suffer greatly; to suffer with or feel another’s pain, condole”), from Latin con- (prefix denoting a being or bringing together of several things) + doleō (“to suffe

parole.significato: Contempt for worldly concerns or secular life.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin contemptus mundī (literally “contempt for the world”), as used in works such as Bernard of Cluny’s De contemptu mundi. First attested in the mid-19th century in English.

parole.significato: A lay brother.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin conversus.

parole.significato: A monk's hood that can be pulled forward to cover the face; a robe with such a hood attached to it.
parole.testo: From Middle English coule, from Old English cūle, from earlier cugele (“hood, cowl”), from Ecclesiastical Latin cuculla (“monk's cowl”), from Latin cucullus (“hood”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of cagoule.

parole.significato: A designated minister of charity in the early Church (see Acts 6:1-6).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English deken, dekne, from Old English diacon, from Ecclesiastical Latin diāconus, from Ancient Greek διᾱ́κονος (diā́konos, “servant, minister”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a religious order that historically forswore the wearing of shoes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin discalceātus (“barefoot”) + -ed, rendering French déchaussé. By surface analysis, dis- + calced.

parole.significato: The mass of a rocket including its contents but without propellant.
parole.testo: From dry + mass. In the liturgical sense, a calque of Ecclesiastical Latin missa sicca.

parole.significato: A church council to which bishops from the entire world are invited, held by Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Christ…
parole.testo: Calque of Ecclesiastical Latin oecūmenicum concilium.

parole.significato: The state of the human nature of Jesus Christ being entirely dependent on, and not existing independently of, the divin…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin enhypostasia, from Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”) + ὑπόστασις (hupóstasis, “existence; essence; substance”) + -ία (-ía, suffix forming nouns). ὑπόστασις is in turn derived from ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, “below, under”) + στάσις (stásis, “standing”). Compare Ancient Greek ἐνυπόστα

parole.significato: A hermit; a religious recluse, someone who lives alone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin eremita, from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs), from ἐρῆμος (erêmos, “uninhabited”) + -ίτης (-ítēs). Doublet of hermit.

parole.significato: In the Byzantine Empire, a governor of a distant province.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin exarchus.

parole.significato: To officially exclude someone from membership of a church or religious community.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin excommunicātus, perfect passive participle of excommunicō (“excommunicate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, ex- + communicate.

parole.significato: Excommunicated.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin excommunicātus, perfect passive participle of excommunicō (“put out of the community”). See -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more. Displaced native Old English āmǣnsumian.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to expiation.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin expiātōrius.

parole.significato: A weekday on a Church calendar on which no feast is observed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin fēria.

parole.significato: The teaching or expression of an opinion in the conscious knowledge that it is contradictory to the teachings of the Ch…
parole.testo: Calque of Ecclesiastical Latin haeresis fōrmālis.

parole.significato: A member of a certain group of descendants of Canaan who inhabited the land of Canaan.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin Gergeseum, from Ancient Greek Γεργεσαῖον (Gergesaîon), from Biblical Hebrew גִּרְגָּשִׁי (girgāšî). Further etymology is unknown.

parole.significato: The first section of the Christian New Testament scripture, comprising the books of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, conce…
parole.testo: From Middle English gospel, gospell, godspel, godspell, goddspell, from Old English godspell (“gospel”), corresponding to God + spell (“talk, tale, story”), literally “the message of God”, believed to be an alteration of earlier *gōdspell (literally “good news”), used to translate ecclesiastical Lat

parole.significato: Used by the Vatican to announce the election of a new Pope.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin habēmus pāpam (literally “we have a pope”).

parole.significato: A sedimentary deposit, especially in urine.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin hypostasis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόστασις (hupóstasis, “sediment, foundation; substance, existence, essence”), from ὑπό (hupó, “under”) + στάσις (stásis, “standing”). Morphologically hypo- + -stasis.

parole.significato: To the highest degree; archetypal, quintessential.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin in excelsīs (“on high, in the highest”), as in the Gloria.

parole.significato: Of a bishop or see: merely titular, without regular jurisdiction, and serving to assist some other bishop or to act as…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin in partibus īnfidēlium (literally “in the regions of the infidels”), so named because such bishops were assigned sees corresponding to territories that had passed under the control of other religions, and so did not imply a duty of residence or diocesan responsibil

parole.significato: Embodied in flesh; given a bodily, especially a human, form; personified.
parole.testo: First attested in 1395, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English incarnat(e) (“(of God or Christ) embodied in human form or flesh, incarnate; provided with new tissues, healed; (with devel, in curses) bloody”), borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātus, perfect passive participle of inca

parole.significato: To embody in flesh; to invest with a bodily, especially a human, form.
parole.testo: First attested in 1533; borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: The prayers spoken by the priest at the foot of the altar at the start of a Tridentine Mass.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin introībō ad altāre Deī (“I shall go in towards the altar of God”), the first line spoken.

parole.significato: the hundredth psalm (ninety-ninth in the Vulgate); the music to which it is set.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin jūbilāte (“rejoice!, shout ye!”), second-person plural present active imperative of jūbilō, the first word of the psalm in Latin.

parole.significato: A short prayer or petition including the phrase kyrie eleison, meaning “Lord, have mercy”.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin Kyrie, contraction of the Ancient Greek phrase Κύριε ἐλέησον (Kúrie eléēson, “Lord, have mercy”), from Ancient Greek Κύριε (Kúrie), vocative form of Κύριος (Kúrios, “Lord”), from κῦρος (kûros, “supremacy, authority”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱēw-, *ḱewh₁- (“to swell, spre

parole.significato: A book or listing that contains a collection of scripture readings appointed for Christian or Jewish worship on a given…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin lēctiōnārium.

parole.significato: One who willingly accepts being put to death or willingly accepts challenging and exposing iniquity done to oneself for…
parole.testo: From Middle English martir, from Old English martyr, itself a borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin martyr, from Ancient Greek μάρτυρ (mártur), later form of μάρτυς (mártus, “witness”).

parole.significato: A tomb or other edifice erected in homage to a martyr.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin martyrium, from Ancient Greek μαρτύριον (martúrion, “testimony”). Equivalent to martyr + -ium.

parole.significato: An opinion that is objectively contradictory to the teachings of the Church, and as such heretical, but which is uttere…
parole.testo: Calque of Ecclesiastical Latin haeresis māteriālis.

parole.significato: a mass, in the sense of a composition setting several sung parts of the liturgical service (most often chosen from the…
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin missa (“mass”).

parole.significato: One who rules over mysteries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin mystēriarchēs (“one who presides over Christian sacraments”), from Ancient Greek μυστηριάρχης (mustēriárkhēs, “one who rules over religious mysteries”), from μυστήριον (mustḗrion) + -άρχης (-árkhēs), corresponding to mystery + -arch.

parole.significato: A recitation of prayers and devotions for nine consecutive days, especially one to a saint to ask for their intercessio…
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin novēna, from Latin novēnus (“nine [each]”).

parole.significato: To set one's eyes upon, glaze at, behold.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin oculātus, perfect passive participle of oculō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Describing a doctrine or proposition that is not heretical, but formulated improperly or ambiguously and hence liable t…
parole.testo: Calque of Ecclesiastical Latin piārum aurium offēnsīvus.

parole.significato: An indulgence that remits part of a person’s sins, and thus part of their time in purgatory.
parole.testo: From partial + indulgence, a calque of Ecclesiastical Latin indulgentia partiālis.

parole.significato: Sin that is said to contravene the natural moral order rather than offending God directly, for example because the sinn…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ecclesiastical Latin peccātum philosophicum, coined around 1600.

parole.significato: An indulgence that remits all of a person’s sins, and thus the whole of their time in purgatory.
parole.testo: From plenary + indulgence, a calque of Ecclesiastical Latin indulgentia plēnāria.

parole.significato: The concluding portion of the communion service.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin postcommūniō. By surface analysis, post- + communion.

parole.significato: The first Sunday after Easter Sunday.
parole.testo: From the opening of the introit of the day’s Tridentine Mass in Ecclesiastical Latin: quasi modo genitī īnfāntēs (“as newborn babes …”).

parole.significato: Describing a council convoked by the emperor Justinian II at Constantinople in 692, also known as the Council in Trullo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin quīnisextus.

parole.significato: A Jewish scholar or teacher of halacha (Jewish law), capable of making halachic decisions.
parole.testo: From Middle English raby, from Ecclesiastical Latin rabbi, and its source Koine Greek ῥαββί (rhabbí), from (post-Tanakh) Hebrew רַבִּי (rabbi, “my master”), from רַב (rav, “master”) + ־ִי (-í, “my”). Compare late Old English rabbi. Doublet of rebbe and related to rav.

parole.significato: An ancient book of the Roman Catholic Church, containing the rites for Mass, the sacraments, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin sacramentarium; compare French sacramentaire.

parole.significato: A class of monk in Catholic belief who dwelt in his own home, or in or near a city.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin sarabaita, possibly from Coptic ⲥⲁ (sa) + ⲣⲁⲩⲏ (rauē) or Coptic ⲥⲁ (sa) + ⲣⲁ (ra) + ⲁⲩⲏⲧ (auēt). Compare with ⲥⲁⲣⲁⲕⲱⲧⲉ (sarakōte).

parole.significato: A position that requires little to no work, or easy work, but still gives an ample payment; a cushy job.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin sine cūrā (literally “without care”), ellipsis of beneficium sine cūrā (“benefice without cure [of souls, i.e. the office of a curate]”), formed from Medieval Latin sine (“without”) + cūrā (“care, charge, cure”).

parole.significato: An inhabitant of the city of Šianu (identified with modern Siano on the coast of Syria).
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin Sineum, from Ancient Greek Ασενναῖον (Asennaîon), from Biblical Hebrew סִינִי (sînî).

parole.significato: To oversee the work of others; to supervise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin superintendō.

parole.significato: A person who is authorized to supervise, direct or administer something.
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin superintendens, a calque of Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos); thence being distantly related to English bishop.

parole.significato: A cycle of texts to be read or chanted at liturgical services on particular weeks and movable feasts throughout the yea…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin temporāle, substantivisation of temporālis (“of or pertaining to time”).

parole.significato: The Pope.
parole.testo: Calque of Ecclesiastical Latin vicārius Christī.

parole.significato: An inhabitant of the city of Ṣumuru (identified with modern Tell Kazel on the coast of Syria).
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin Samariten, from Ancient Greek Σαμαραῖον (Samaraîon), from Hebrew צְמָרִי (ṣᵊmārî).

parole.significato: Sunday, the first day of the week, particularly as the Christian Sabbath.
parole.testo: A calque of Ecclesiastical Latin diēs Dominicus, either directly or as a later development of Old Norse dróttinsdagr (“Lord's day”)
